description: The CS Department offers a limited number of Course Assistant (CA), Teaching Assistant (TA), and Research Assistant (RA) appointments. Typical CA responsibilities may include assisting with preparation for lectures or lab activities; conducting labs or review sessions; holding office hours; responding to student questions; assisting with course logistics; monitoring course websites or discussion boards; proctoring exams; and grading assignments, quizzes, exams, or projects in accordance with instructor guidance. TA responsibilities include all CA duties plus additional teaching responsibilities such as preparing for and presenting new material in class sections or labs. Appointments are made for the full quarter (Autumn Oct 1-Dec 31, Winter Jan 1-Mar 31, Spring Apr 1-Jun 30, Summer Jul 1-Sep 30).
notes: Standing/recurring quarterly hiring program rather than a single dated posting. No pay rate is stated anywhere on the fetched page - appointments are described only by percentage (25% = 10 hrs/wk, 50% = 20 hrs/wk), so pay is left null rather than guessed. The application portal https://caapp.cs.stanford.edu/ redirects to Stanford SSO (login.stanford.edu) and could not be read without credentials. A separate ACE (Additional Calculus for Engineers) CA process exists with an earlier timeline, per the same page. Evidence fetched 2026-08-31; the page's FAQ links to AY 26-27 application dates.

The Stanford CS Department's CA/RA page states: 'Undergraduate students are not eligible to be CA's, however, do have the option to be paid Section Leaders. More information about section leading can be found on the CS198 website.' (source: https://cs.stanford.edu/masters-course-assistant-and-research-assistant)
description: The CS198 program consists of ~100 undergraduate and a handful of graduate students who teach section, grade coursework, and assist students in office hours for Stanford's introductory CS courses CS106A, CS106B and CS106L. The program gives qualified undergraduate students of all majors a unique opportunity to teach as part of their Stanford experience. Section leaders cover materials such as the C++ and Python programming languages, functional decomposition, algorithms, recursion, abstract data types, algorithmic analysis, data structure design, and other fundamental elements of modern programming. Per the CS198 recruiting deck, section leaders teach a weekly 1-hour section, help students in the LaIR, grade CS106 assignments, hold IGs (individual grading meetings) with students, and grade midterms and finals.
notes: STANDING/RECURRING role, not a dated posting. IMPORTANT PROVENANCE CAVEAT: the public cs198.stanford.edu landing page (fetched 2026-08-31) contains only the program description and the cs198@cs.stanford.edu contact; everything past it (/web/auth, and the legacy /cs198/Apply.aspx which now redirects to /web) is behind Stanford SSO, so no live application window or current pay rate could be read. The requirements and duties above marked with source_url = the CS110 handouts PDF come from https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs110/handouts/cs198-section-leading-slides.pdf, which I fetched and text-extracted in this task. That deck states 'Get paid $18.50/hour (more with seniority)' and a deadline of 'Thursday, January 27th at 11:59PM PT'. The deck carries no year; January 27 last fell on a Thursday in 2022, and it names Marissa Mayer as 'Former CEO, Yahoo', so it is very likely several years old. I therefore left pay null rather than publish $18.50/hr as a current rate - a student should confirm the current rate with cs198@cs.stanford.edu. A WebSearch result summary also asserted 'Applications to section lead in Spring 2026 are now open' and repeated the $18.50/hour figure, but I could not verify either claim on a page I fetched, so neither is recorded as fact.

description: Oral Communication Tutors (OCTs) are peer speaking tutors who support students at all stages of the oral presentation process. OCTs work with graduate and undergraduate students from a variety of academic disciplines to brainstorm, organize, and rehearse oral presentations, on issues including structure, delivery, voice, pacing, non-verbal communication, effective use of visual aids, interviewing skills, and overcoming speech anxiety. OCTs work with students during individual consultations in the Hume Center and in classes that emphasize instruction in oral presentation, e.g. PWR2 classes and WR2 seminars. There are also opportunities for interested OCTs to develop and conduct workshops.

The Specialist staffs public service desks, assists patrons with locating materials and navigating the library catalog, processes routine circulation transactions, backs up the Welcome Desk with visitor registration and bag inspections, supports the Media Center (microfilm, DVDs, video games), picks requested books from the stacks, processes new materials, supports collection management projects, and may retrieve and scan materials for interlibrary lending and digital delivery.
notes: FETCH NOTE ON THIS CATEGORY: Stanford Libraries publishes NO public student-assistant hiring page. I fetched library.stanford.edu and its full sitemap.xml (1,216 URLs, fetched 2026-08-31) and found no jobs/employment/careers/student-employment page; library.stanford.edu/about/jobs, /jobs, /about/employment and /work-us all return HTTP 404. The legacy careersearch.stanford.edu/jobs/... URLs surfaced by web search (e.g. 'Library Welcome Desk Attendant (Portal Monitor)') all return HTTP 404 - that site has migrated to Oracle HCM. I therefore queried the live Oracle HCM requisition API and this record is drawn from requisition 200761, ExternalPostedStartDate 2026-08-19T01:19:36+00:00. No pay range appears anywhere in the requisition's fetched external description, so pay is null - the $18-$26/hr and $26.97-$32.54/hr figures that appeared in web-search snippets came from Glassdoor and a stale 404'd posting and are NOT recorded. description: This project investigates how individuals adapt their help-seeking strategies to social partners of varying reliability. The lab designed 'CodeBreaker,' a Mastermind-style online game in which participants guess secret color codes and can request clues from a partner who may or may not respond. By varying the partner's reliability and the difficulty and stakes of each game, the team measures when people ask for help, persist on their own, or opt into harder challenges. Data will be collected from adults online. The RA will be involved in the full research cycle: helping refine and extend the experimental paradigm (configuring new game conditions and helper behaviors, piloting and QA-testing changes before launch - the game is a web app built in React/TypeScript with a Node.js backend, and most experimental changes require only editing configuration files, so deep web-development experience is not required); running online data collection with adults on Prolific (setting up and monitoring studies, handling participant communication and bonus payments, performing data-quality checks); analyzing the resulting behavioral data in R or Python; and meeting weekly with the research team.
